commands.name: dataviz
commands.description: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".

commands.name: update-config
commands.description: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

commands.name: verify
commands.description: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Run before committing nontrivial changes; bootstraps this repo's project verify skill if none exists yet. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

commands.description: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's review recipe covers them) at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. commands.name: anthropic-skills:docx
commands.description: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx) or Word templates (.dotx). Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, page numbers, or letterheads. Also use when extracting or reorganizing content from .docx or .dotx files, inserting or replacing images in documents, find-and-replace in Word files, working with tracked changes or comments, or converting content into a polished Word document. If the user asks for a 'report', 'memo', 'letter', 'template', or similar deliverable as a Word or .docx file (to download, email or print), use this skill. However, if they ask for a document, page, report, memo, or notes WITHOUT naming a file format and the session offers Claude's own dedicated document or page skill or connector, use that instead. Do NOT use for PDFs, spreadsheets, Google Docs, or coding unrelated to document generation. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: anthropic-skills:import-memory
commands.description: Import a memory export from another AI assistant into Claude's memory — conversationally, additively, and with the content treated as data. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: anthropic-skills:morning
commands.description: Render the user's morning brief as a styled HTML artifact, or set it up as a recurring weekday task. Use only when the user explicitly asks to run, see, or set up their morning brief, or if they invoke /morning by name. A question about their day, schedule, or calendar is not by itself a request for the brief; answer it directly instead. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: anthropic-skills:pdf
commands.description: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. This includes reading or extracting text/tables from PDFs, combining or merging multiple PDFs into one, splitting PDFs apart, rotating pages, adding watermarks, creating new PDFs, filling PDF forms, encrypting/decrypting PDFs, extracting images, and OCR on scanned PDFs to make them searchable. If the user mentions a .pdf file or asks to produce one, use this skill. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: anthropic-skills:pptx
commands.description: Use this skill any time a .pptx or .potx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations as PowerPoint (.pptx) files; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx or .potx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email, summary, or creating a different type of slide deck); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates (.potx), layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user asks for a PowerPoint or .pptx file, or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. However, when the user asks for a deck, slides, a slide deck, or a presentation without naming a file format, default to using a dedicated slide-deck artifact type or a separate slides skill if this session offers one; otherwise, use this skill. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: anthropic-skills:skill-creator
commands.description: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy. (claude.ai sync)

commands.name: anthropic-skills:xlsx
commands.description: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Trigger especially when the user references a spreadsheet file by name or path — even casually (like "the xlsx in my downloads") — and wants something done to it or produced from it. Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved. (claude.ai sync)

concept TaskTableConcept:
    pitch:
        The output of one run of the harness, as a table of everything it did,
        filling in as it does it.

    shape: {TaskTableShape}

shape TaskTableShape:
    description:
        A table with Type, Output, and Status columns, with one row per thing
        the harness did, in order: each piece of reply text, each tool call, and
        any error. It is the same table wherever a run's output is shown, a
        task, a question, a previous task or answer, the palette's search for a
        file, or a run in one of the application's own panels, and each use
        says where it sits.

    types:
        Type is a coloured badge with an icon. Reply text is "Reply" and errors
        are "Error". Tool calls are "Files" for Read, Glob, Grep, LS, and
        NotebookRead; "Edit" for Edit, MultiEdit, Write, and NotebookEdit;
        "Command" for Bash, BashOutput, KillShell, and KillBash; "Web" for
        WebFetch and WebSearch; "Agent" for Task and Agent; and "Tool" for
        anything else.

    status:
        A tool call's status is "running", "done", or "failed", and a call still
        running when the run ends takes the state the run ended in.

    replies:
        Reply text is rendered as markdown, with no border around it. What
        subagents do is left out. If nothing streamed but the harness reports a
        final result, that result is shown as the reply. A finished run with
        nothing to show reads "No output."

    toolCalls:
        A tool call's Output cell shows its most telling argument. For Files,
        Edit, Command, Web, and Agent calls the tool's name is left out, since
        the badge already says what it is; any other tool's name comes first.

        Any path inside the project directory is shown relative to it, and the
        project directory itself reads `.`.

        A command is shown whole, as a syntax-highlighted bash block, and a long
        one is split across lines at `&&`, `||`, `|`, and `;`, one command per
        line with the chained ones indented. It never splits inside quotes,
        command substitutions, brackets, comments, or heredocs. Other arguments
        are shown on a single line.

    streaming:
        While the run is under way, the table ends in a waiting row for
        whatever the harness does next. Until a row has something meaningful to
        show, its Type cell is a skeleton and its Output cell shows the last
        three lines of the harness's raw JSON output: muted, monospace, JSON
        syntax-highlighted, and always three lines tall so the row doesn't jump.

from /scope/application/MainWindow import MainWindowScope

export scope ThemeScope:
    concept: {ThemeConcept}

concept ThemeConcept:
    pitch:
        The look every part of the application shares: a gentle, neutral grey
        interface in the manner of Photoshop, Maya, or Houdini, where contrast
        alone says what matters, and colour is kept for meaning.

    shape: {ThemeShape}

shape ThemeShape:
    description:
        The theme is defined by its dark mode, built around a base grey of
        #444444. Dark mode is the reference: every colour below is chosen for
        it first, and light mode is its reasonable interpretation on a light
        base, keeping the same roles, the same order, and steps of about the
        same size. The greys are true neutrals, with no hint of blue or warmth.
        There are no gradients, and no texture. Everything that uses a colour
        names its role here rather than a value of its own, so the two modes
        stay coherent.

    hierarchy:
        How far a colour is from the base, in contrast, says how much it stands
        out, and that holds everywhere. The base is the quiet ground of the
        window. A step away is structure: panels, controls, and the lines
        between them. Further away is what is worked on: text, content, and the
        wells that hold it. Furthest away is state and meaning: what is
        selected, focused, or needs attention. Nothing structural is ever
        further from the base than the content it frames, and nothing decorative
        is ever as far as state. A hover is always a smaller step than a
        selection, and a selection a smaller step than focus.

    surfaces:
        Each surface in dark mode, then light mode:
        - well, #2e2e2e, then #f5f5f5: where content is read or written, such as the editor, code blocks, answers, and task tables' bodies; the most contrast with the text it holds
        - recessed, #383838, then #e8e8e8: text inputs, lists, and trees, a step toward the well
        - base, #444444, then #d0d0d0: the window, its panels, the sidebar, and the ribbon's command area
        - raised, #4e4e4e, then #dadada: buttons, tab bars, headers, a group's title strip, and cards, a small step toward the viewer
        - hover, #585858, then #e2e2e2: a raised or listed thing under the pointer, one step further along the way it is already raised
        - pressed, #3c3c3c, then #c6c6c6: a control held down, a step back past the base
        - selected, #5e5e5e, then #bcbcbc: a selected row or tab without focus, the neutral state furthest from its surface short of the accent
        - overlay, #4a4a4a, then #dcdcdc: floating surfaces, such as menus, popovers, tooltips, the completion menu, and inset panels

    lightMode:
        Light mode reads the dark ladder on a light base of #d0d0d0. Wells and
        inputs go lighter, toward white, so they keep the most contrast with the
        dark text they hold, just as they are darker in dark mode for the same
        reason. Raised controls and floating surfaces go a smaller step lighter
        too, so they still come forward, and hover goes further the same way.
        Pressed and selected go darker, and so do lines. Text is dark on light.

    text:
        Text in dark mode, then light mode:
        - primary, #ebebeb, then #1e1e1e: the foreground, for anything read
        - secondary, #c4c4c4, then #454545: what the spec calls muted, such as paths, counts, and descriptions
        - tertiary, #9c9c9c, then #636363: dimmer than muted, such as help text and placeholders
        - disabled, #7a7a7a, then #8c8c8c: what can't be used now

    lines:
        Lines are one pixel, and quieter than anything they separate:
        - line, #3a3a3a, then #bdbdbd: dividers between areas, table rows, and list rows
        - edge, #2a2a2a, then #a6a6a6: the border of controls, inputs, and floating surfaces, darker than the base in both modes, what the spec calls the border colour

        A line is never doubled. Wherever two things that each have a border
        meet, a single line is drawn between them, never two side by side:
        one of them leaves that side out, or the two overlap so their lines lie
        on the same pixels. A thing that fills what holds it leaves out the
        sides the holder already draws, and a row in a stack draws only the
        line between it and the row before. This holds while things move too,
        such as a row sliding into a stack, apart from a frame or two. A focus
        ring, or an accent bar marking what is current, isn't a border in this
        sense, and may sit against one. A gpui-kit component used with its
        default styling, such as tabs in a tab bar, keeps its own borders as
        gpui-kit draws them; only its colours are the theme's.

    accent:
        One accent, a calm blue, is the only colour that means selection,
        focus, or the primary action:
        - accent, #7fb4ea, then #1f5fa6: focus rings, the underline of a selected tab, links, a selection's edge, and accent text
        - accent fill, #3d6a98, then #2b68ad: primary buttons, with primary text in white in both modes, and a selected item in a focused list
        - selection, the accent fill at 35% over its surface: selected text

        What the spec calls the theme's primary colour, or its focus ring
        colour, is the accent.

    status:
        Status colours are kept for what they mean, readable as text on the base
        and every surface darker than it in dark mode, and on the base and every
        surface lighter than it in light mode:
        - success, #8fd095, then #2c6e31: done, added, aligned
        - warning, #e6bb68, then #8a5a00: running out, modified, drifting
        - error, #f0928a, then #b3261e: failed, removed, diverged
        - information, the accent: running, informational notes

        Two more hues, for telling kinds of things apart rather than for status:
        - purple, #bba0e6, then #6b4aa6
        - cyan, #78c8ce, then #1f6f78

        Wherever the spec names a hue for what is shown, it means the theme's:
        blue is the accent, green success, amber or yellow warning, red error,
        purple and cyan the hues above, and grey tertiary text.

        A tint of a colour, such as a prompt mode's or a changed line's, is that
        colour laid over its surface at low strength, never enough to take the

    concept: {TaskTableConcept}

concept TaskTableConcept:
    pitch:
        The output of one run of the harness, as a table of everything it did,
        filling in as it does it.

    shape: {TaskTableShape}

shape TaskTableShape:
    description:
        A table with Type, Output, and Status columns, with one row per thing
        the harness did, in order: each piece of reply text, each tool call, and
        any error. It is the same table wherever a run's output is shown, a
        task, a question, a previous task or answer, the palette's search for a
        file, or a run in one of the application's own panels, and each use
        says where it sits.

    types:
        Type is a coloured badge with an icon. Reply text is "Reply" and errors
        are "Error". Tool calls are "Files" for Read, Glob, Grep, LS, and
        NotebookRead; "Edit" for Edit, MultiEdit, Write, and NotebookEdit;
        "Command" for Bash, BashOutput, KillShell, and KillBash; "Web" for
        WebFetch and WebSearch; "Agent" for Task and Agent; and "Tool" for
        anything else.

    status:
        A tool call's status is "running", "done", or "failed", and a call still
        running when the run ends takes the state the run ended in.

    replies:
        Reply text is rendered as markdown, with no border around it. What
        subagents do is left out. If nothing streamed but the harness reports a
        final result, that result is shown as the reply. A finished run with
        nothing to show reads "No output."

    toolCalls:
        A tool call's Output cell shows its most telling argument. For Files,
        Edit, Command, Web, and Agent calls the tool's name is left out, since
        the badge already says what it is; any other tool's name comes first.

        Any path inside the project directory is shown relative to it, and the
        project directory itself reads `.`.

        A command is shown whole, as a syntax-highlighted bash block, and a long
        one is split across lines at `&&`, `||`, `|`, and `;`, one command per
        line with the chained ones indented. It never splits inside quotes,
        command substitutions, brackets, comments, or heredocs. Other arguments
        are shown on a single line.

    streaming:
        While the run is under way, the table ends in a waiting row for
        whatever the harness does next. Until a row has something meaningful to
        show, its Type cell is a skeleton and its Output cell shows the last
        three lines of the harness's raw JSON output: muted, monospace, JSON
        syntax-highlighted, and always three lines tall so the row doesn't jump.
        Before any output has arrived it reads "Waiting for the harness…". As
        soon as a row's type is known, its badge is real, and as soon as its
        text or argument arrives, that is shown. While the input of a Files,
        Edit, Command, Web, or Agent call is still arriving, its Output cell
        shows only a skeleton.

        A skeleton stands in for a running row only while there is nothing
        meaningful to show for it. As soon as there is, no skeleton is shown for
        it at all.

    scrolling:
        The rows scroll beneath the table's header, which stays at the top,
        with a @{ScrollbarScope}, usually with its lock to the bottom. Locked,
        the table follows the run's latest output. Unlocked, it still follows
        new output while it is already scrolled to the bottom, and stays put
        once scrolled away from it. Each use says whether its table has the
        lock, and whether it starts on.

        However long the output grows, drawing it costs no more than drawing
        the rows in view, so scrolling, animations, and new output stay smooth.
        While the end of the table is scrolled out of view, raw output that
        would only change the waiting row redraws nothing.

    collapsedSteps:
        A use can say its table collapses the steps leading up to the answer,
        once the run is finished. The steps are every row up to and including
        the harness's last tool call; the answer is the rows after it. In their
        place, the table's first row reads "Show 1 step" or "Show N steps",
        muted, beside a right chevron, with the answer beneath it. A single
        click on that row expands the steps in place, above the answer, and the
        row then reads "Hide 1 step" or "Hide N steps" beside a down chevron;
        clicking it again collapses them. Each table is expanded or collapsed on
        its own.

        A run with no tool calls, or with nothing after its last one, has
        nothing to collapse and shows whole. A run still under way shows its
        latest step as usual.

    legibility:
        The output from a realtime agent should be readable and meaningful.
        Make sure the font size is large enough, and that the colours are
        legible in both light and dark mode.
